intro: Norbert Schenk plays the organ of the Evangelische Kirche in Solms-Albshausen in a recording dated 2017. His complete performance is available, while the orchestral comparison is restricted to the opening carried on Stokowski’s first disc side.
question: What changes when the same gestures remain on one organ rather than passing through an orchestra?

cues.title: An identified church organ
cues.text: The source identifies Norbert Schenk and the Evangelische Kirche in Solms-Albshausen, Hessen. Schenk explicitly released the recording under CC BY 4.0; 2017 is the recording year, not the later permission date.
cues.evidence: Commons quotes Schenk’s release, dated 10 March 2020, and gives the recording date as 2017.

cues.title: After the opening weight
cues.text: The opening’s stronger sustained sound gives way to a more active surface. Compare the way the organ connects these gestures with the orchestral change of weight.
cues.evidence: The 0:24 boundary follows a high-level 0:15 window with few detected attacks; by 0:25 there are about 3 detected attacks per second.

cues.title: Continuing beyond the comparison
cues.text: The organ performance continues after the aligned opening. Follow the moving lines within its sustained sound, but do not expect a simultaneous position on the shorter Stokowski source side.
cues.evidence: The complete organ file lasts 464 seconds; the comparison trim ends at 128 seconds. No later passage correspondence is claimed.

cues.title: A quieter continuing texture
cues.text: This later stretch has less recorded weight than the surrounding passages while its activity continues. Try following a lower line independently of the upper movement.
cues.evidence: The 4:00–4:15 windows sit around −21 dB with 1.8–3.6 detected attacks per second; this listening invitation does not identify a separated organ voice.

cues.title: Broader closing gestures
cues.text: The closing region replaces a busier surface with longer stretches between attacks. Follow how the sustained notes occupy the church’s resonance before quicker activity returns.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 6:22, 6:26 and 6:34 surround windows with 0.2–0.4 detected attacks per second; activity increases to 5.4 at 6:40.

cues.title: Resonance and silence
cues.text: The final sound decays before the file finishes. The duration of that tail belongs to the recording as well as to the performer’s final release.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −6.9 dB at 7:25 to −19.2 at 7:30, −71.2 at 7:35 and −80 at 7:40.

facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players

composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
